name: Mint leaf
lede: Mint leaf is a clear, light yellowish green dated to Ridgway's 1912 color nomenclature, and despite the garden-herb name it is one of the rarest colors in our painting archive.

sections.title: A garden word, a rare paint
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature lists this tone, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 places it in block 135, "deep yellowish green", 3.8 units from that block's center [1]. In the ColorHub library the same point is also carried under Cendre Green, an exact duplicate (ΔE 0.0) [1][3]. The books held in color-kb have no entry for "Mint leaf" [4].

Its nearest distinct neighbor is [[neuwieder-green]], 3.1 units off, "almost the same" by our graph [3]. Nearby cousins in the library include [[cobalt-green]] and [[dark-sea-green]], both duller or more saturated versions of the same yellow-green family [3].

The gap between a common garden word and a rare painted color is itself a finding: not every plant name used by dye and paint catalogers in 1912 reflects how often painters actually reached for that hue [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Despite its plant-garden name, Mint leaf is nearly absent from our archive: 5 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.02 percent, as photographed [2]. The handful that do carry it include two Van Gogh still lifes and a Mughal portrait of Emperor Jahangir, where it covers over half the canvas [2]. Counts are computed matches on varnished, photographed paintings, not pigment identifications [2].
